name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_MCQI_DUALNATUREOFRADIATIONANDMATTER_MCQ_Q11_1 - De Broglie wavelength of falling particle

questiontext.text: 11.1 A particle is dropped from a height \(H\). The de Broglie wavelength of the particle as a function of height is proportional to

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
A particle of mass \(m\) is dropped from rest (initial speed \(u = 0\)) from a height \(H\) under uniform gravitational acceleration \(g\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
Air resistance is neglected and the motion is non-relativistic, with downward displacement taken as positive.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
For free fall from rest through a height \(H\), the speed \(v\) is given by the kinematic relation \(v^2 = u^2 + 2gH\). The de Broglie wavelength \(\lambda\) of a particle of momentum \(p = mv\) is \(\lambda = \frac{h}{p} = \frac{h}{mv}\), where \(h\) is Planck's constant.

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Substituting \(u = 0\) into the kinematic equation gives \(v = \sqrt{2gH}\). Substituting this speed into the de Broglie relation yields \(\lambda = \frac{h}{m\sqrt{2gH}} = \left(\frac{h}{m\sqrt{2g}}\right) H^{-1/2}\). Since \(h\), \(m\), and \(g\) are constants for the given particle, \(\lambda \propto H^{-1/2}\).

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Dimensionally, as \(H\) increases, the speed increases and the de Broglie wavelength decreases, consistent with a negative exponent. Therefore, the de Broglie wavelength is proportional to \(H^{-1/2}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_MCQI_DUALNATUREOFRADIATIONANDMATTER_MCQ_Q11_2 - Photon wavelength to remove bound proton

questiontext.text: 11.2 The wavelength of a photon needed to remove a proton from a nucleus which is bound to the nucleus with \(1\text{ MeV}\) energy is nearly

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Binding energy of the proton in the nucleus, \(E = 1\text{ MeV} = 10^{6}\text{ eV}\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
The minimum energy required by the photon to just remove the proton is equal to the binding energy \(E\). Standard constant values are \(h = 6.626 \times 10^{-34}\text{ J}\cdot\text{s}\), \(c = 3 \times 10^{8}\text{ m/s}\), and \(1\text{ eV} = 1.6 \times 10^{-19}\text{ J}\), giving \(hc \approx 1240\text{ eV}\cdot\text{nm}\).

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
The energy of a photon of wavelength \(\lambda\) is \(E = \frac{hc}{\lambda}\), so \(\lambda = \frac{hc}{E}\).

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Substituting the given energy: \(\lambda = \frac{1240\text{ eV}\cdot\text{nm}}{10^{6}\text{ eV}} = 1.24 \times 10^{-3}\text{ nm} \approx 1.2 \times 10^{-3}\text{ nm}\).

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
A \(1\text{ MeV}\) photon lies in the gamma-ray region, which has wavelengths on the order of \(10^{-3}\text{ nm}\) (\(10^{-12}\text{ m}\)). Thus, the required wavelength is nearly \(1.2 \times 10^{-3}\text{ nm}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_MCQI_DUALNATUREOFRADIATIONANDMATTER_MCQ_Q11_3 - Electron beam incident on metal surface

questiontext.text: 11.3 Consider a beam of electrons (each electron with energy \(E_0\)) incident on a metal surface kept in an evacuated chamber. Then

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
When an energetic beam of electrons strikes a metal surface, the incident electrons interact with the free and bound electrons of the metal through elastic and inelastic collisions, causing back-scattering of primary electrons and ejection of secondary electrons.

Step 2: Evaluation
Unlike photons in the photoelectric effect (where a photon is completely absorbed and the maximum kinetic energy of an emitted electron is \(h\nu - \phi\)), an incident electron is not absorbed as a whole; it can scatter elastically from the surface retaining virtually all of its initial energy \(E_0\), or it can lose any fraction of its energy in inelastic collisions before emerging or knocking out secondary electrons.

Step 3: Application
Because electrons can undergo any number of collisions and lose varying amounts of energy, the emitted electrons (both scattered primary and secondary electrons) can emerge with a continuous range of energies from zero up to the maximum possible value \(E_0\).

Step 4: Final Conclusion
Therefore, electrons can be emitted with any energy, with a maximum of \(E_0\).

answer.text: no electrons will be emitted as only photons can emit electrons.
electrons can be emitted but all with an energy, \(E_0\).
electrons can be emitted with any energy, with a maximum of \(E_0 - \phi\) (\(\phi\) is the work function).
electrons can be emitted with any energy, with a maximum of \(E_0\).

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_MCQI_DUALNATUREOFRADIATIONANDMATTER_MCQ_Q11_4 - Davisson Germer diffraction angle with voltage

questiontext.text: 11.4 Consider Fig. 11.7 in the NCERT text book of physics for Class XII. Suppose the voltage applied to A is increased. The diffracted beam will have the maximum at a value of \(\theta\) that

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
In the Davisson–Germer experiment (Fig. 11.7 of the NCERT Class XII Physics textbook), electrons are accelerated through a potential difference \(V\) applied to the accelerating anode and diffracted by a nickel crystal, with diffraction maxima governed by Bragg's law.

Step 2: Evaluation
The de Broglie wavelength of electrons accelerated through potential \(V\) is \(\lambda = \frac{h}{\sqrt{2meV}}\), so increasing \(V\) decreases \(\lambda\). According to the diffraction condition \(D \sin\theta = n\lambda\) (or \(2d \sin\alpha = n\lambda\), where the scattering angle \(\theta\) increases with \(\lambda\)), \(\sin\theta\) is directly proportional to \(\lambda\).

Step 3: Application
When the voltage applied is increased, \(\lambda\) decreases, which in turn decreases \(\sin\theta\) and therefore decreases the angle \(\theta\) (in the first quadrant) at which the diffraction maximum occurs.

Step 4: Final Conclusion
Hence, the diffracted beam will have the maximum at a value of \(\theta\) that will be less than the earlier value.

answer.text: will be larger than the earlier value.
will be the same as the earlier value.
will be less than the earlier value.

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_MCQI_DUALNATUREOFRADIATIONANDMATTER_MCQ_Q11_5 - De Broglie wavelengths at same energy

questiontext.text: 11.5 A proton, a neutron, an electron and an \(\alpha\)-particle have same energy. Then their de Broglie wavelengths compare as

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
A proton (\(\mathrm{p}\)), a neutron (\(\mathrm{n}\)), an electron (\(\mathrm{e}\)), and an \(\alpha\)-particle (\(\alpha\)) all have the same kinetic energy \(K\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
The particles are non-relativistic, and the masses of the proton and neutron are taken as approximately equal (\(m_{\mathrm{p}} \approx m_{\mathrm{n}}\)), while \(m_{\mathrm{e}} \ll m_{\mathrm{p}}\) and \(m_{\alpha} \approx 4m_{\mathrm{p}}\).

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
The de Broglie wavelength of a particle of mass \(m\) and kinetic energy \(K\) is \(\lambda = \frac{h}{p} = \frac{h}{\sqrt{2mK}}\).

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Since \(K\) is identical for all four particles, \(\lambda \propto \frac{1}{\sqrt{m}}\). Ordering the masses gives \(m_{\mathrm{e}} < m_{\mathrm{p}} \approx m_{\mathrm{n}} < m_{\alpha}\). Taking the inverse square roots reverses the inequality: \(\lambda_{\alpha} < \lambda_{\mathrm{p}} = \lambda_{\mathrm{n}} < \lambda_{\mathrm{e}}\).

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
The \(\alpha\)-particle has the largest mass and therefore the shortest de Broglie wavelength, the proton and neutron have equal masses and equal wavelengths, and the electron has the smallest mass and longest wavelength. (Note: the source paper prints the inequality with a typographical reversal on the electron term in \(\lambda_{\alpha} < \lambda_{\mathrm{p}} = \lambda_{\mathrm{n}} > \lambda_{\mathrm{e}}\), which corresponds to the intended ordering \(\lambda_{\alpha} < \lambda_{\mathrm{p}} = \lambda_{\mathrm{n}} < \lambda_{\mathrm{e}}\).)

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_MCQI_DUALNATUREOFRADIATIONANDMATTER_MCQ_Q11_6 - Electron de Broglie wavelength in magnetic field

questiontext.text: 11.6 An electron is moving with an initial velocity \(\mathbf{v} = v_0\mathbf{i}\) and is in a magnetic field \(\mathbf{B} = B_0\mathbf{j}\). Then it's de Broglie wavelength

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
A charged particle moving in a uniform magnetic field experiences the Lorentz magnetic force \(\mathbf{F} = q(\mathbf{v} \times \mathbf{B})\), which is always perpendicular to the instantaneous velocity \(\mathbf{v}\).

Step 2: Evaluation
Because the magnetic force is perpendicular to the velocity, the instantaneous power delivered is \(P = \mathbf{F} \cdot \mathbf{v} = 0\). Hence, the magnetic field does no work on the electron, and its kinetic energy and speed \(|\mathbf{v}| = v_0\) remain constant.

Step 3: Application
The de Broglie wavelength depends on the magnitude of momentum \(p = mv_0\) via \(\lambda = \frac{h}{p} = \frac{h}{mv_0}\). Since \(m\) and \(v_0\) do not change with time, \(\lambda\) does not change with time.

Step 4: Final Conclusion
Therefore, the de Broglie wavelength of the electron remains constant.

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_MCQI_DUALNATUREOFRADIATIONANDMATTER_MCQ_Q11_7 - Electron de Broglie wavelength in parallel electric field

questiontext.text: 11.7 An electron (mass \(m\)) with an initial velocity \(\mathbf{v} = v_0\mathbf{i}\) (\(v_0 > 0\)) is in an electric field \(\mathbf{E} = -E_0\mathbf{i}\) (\(E_0 = \text{constant} > 0\)). It's de Broglie wavelength at time \(t\) is given by

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
An electron of mass \(m\) and charge \(-e\) has initial velocity \(\mathbf{v}(0) = v_0\mathbf{i}\) (\(v_0 > 0\)) and moves in a uniform electric field \(\mathbf{E} = -E_0\mathbf{i}\) (\(E_0 > 0\)). Its initial de Broglie wavelength is \(\lambda_0 = \frac{h}{mv_0}\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
The motion is non-relativistic and one-dimensional along the \(x\)-axis, with \(\mathbf{i}\) as the unit vector in the positive direction.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
The electric force on the electron is \(\mathbf{F} = -e\mathbf{E}\), acceleration is \(\mathbf{a} = \frac{\mathbf{F}}{m}\), velocity at time \(t\) is \(\mathbf{v}(t) = \mathbf{v}(0) + \mathbf{a}t\), and the de Broglie wavelength is \(\lambda(t) = \frac{h}{m|\mathbf{v}(t)|}\).

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
The force is \(\mathbf{F} = (-e)(-E_0\mathbf{i}) = eE_0\mathbf{i}\), so the acceleration is \(\mathbf{a} = \frac{eE_0}{m}\mathbf{i}\). Thus, the velocity at time \(t\) is \(\mathbf{v}(t) = \left(v_0 + \frac{eE_0}{m}t\right)\mathbf{i} = v_0\left(1 + \frac{eE_0 t}{mv_0}\right)\mathbf{i}\). Substituting the speed \(v(t)\) into the de Broglie relation gives \(\lambda(t) = \frac{h}{mv_0\left(1 + \frac{eE_0 t}{mv_0}\right)} = \frac{\lambda_0}{\left(1 + \frac{eE_0}{m}\frac{t}{v_0}\right)}\).

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
At \(t = 0\), \(\lambda(0) = \lambda_0\), and as \(t\) increases, the electron accelerates and its wavelength decreases. Thus, the de Broglie wavelength at time \(t\) is \(\frac{\lambda_0}{\left(1 + \frac{eE_0}{m}\frac{t}{v_0}\right)}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_MCQI_DUALNATUREOFRADIATIONANDMATTER_MCQ_Q11_8 - Electron de Broglie wavelength in perpendicular electric field

questiontext.text: 11.8 An electron (mass \(m\)) with an initial velocity \(\mathbf{v} = v_0 \hat{\mathbf{i}}\) is in an electric field \(\mathbf{E} = E_0 \hat{\mathbf{j}}\). If \(\lambda_0 = h/mv_0\), it's de Broglie wavelength at time \(t\) is given by

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
An electron of mass \(m\) and charge \(-e\) has initial velocity \(\mathbf{v}(0) = v_0 \hat{\mathbf{i}}\) and moves in a uniform transverse electric field \(\mathbf{E} = E_0 \hat{\mathbf{j}}\), with \(\lambda_0 = \frac{h}{mv_0}\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
The motion is non-relativistic in the \(x\)-\(y\) plane, with orthogonal unit vectors \(\hat{\mathbf{i}}\) and \(\hat{\mathbf{j}}\).

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
The electric force is \(\mathbf{F} = -e\mathbf{E}\), the acceleration is \(\mathbf{a} = \frac{\mathbf{F}}{m}\), the velocity vector is \(\mathbf{v}(t) = \mathbf{v}(0) + \mathbf{a}t\), and the de Broglie wavelength is \(\lambda(t) = \frac{h}{m|\mathbf{v}(t)|}\).

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
The force on the electron is \(\mathbf{F} = -eE_0 \hat{\mathbf{j}}\), giving acceleration \(\mathbf{a} = -\frac{eE_0}{m}\hat{\mathbf{j}}\). Therefore, the velocity at time \(t\) is \(\mathbf{v}(t) = v_0 \hat{\mathbf{i}} - \frac{eE_0 t}{m}\hat{\mathbf{j}}\). Its magnitude is \(|\mathbf{v}(t)| = \sqrt{v_0^2 + \frac{e^2 E_0^2 t^2}{m^2}} = v_0 \sqrt{1 + \frac{e^2 E_0^2 t^2}{m^2 v_0^2}}\). Substituting this speed into the de Broglie formula yields \(\lambda(t) = \frac{h}{mv_0\sqrt{1 + \frac{e^2 E_0^2 t^2}{m^2 v_0^2}}} = \frac{\lambda_0}{\sqrt{1 + \frac{e^2 E_0^2 t^2}{m^2 v_0^2}}}\).

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
At \(t = 0\), \(\lambda(0) = \lambda_0\), and as \(t\) increases, the transverse speed grows so \(\lambda(t)\) decreases. Thus, the de Broglie wavelength at time \(t\) is \(\frac{\lambda_0}{\sqrt{1 + \frac{e^2 E_0^2 t^2}{m^2 v_0^2}}}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_MCQII_DUALNATUREOFRADIATIONANDMATTER_MCQ_Q11_9 - Relativistic corrections for electron de Broglie wavelength

questiontext.text: 11.9 Relativistic corrections become necessary when the expression for the kinetic energy \(\frac{1}{2}mv^2\), becomes comparable with \(mc^2\), where \(m\) is the mass of the particle. At what de Broglie wavelength will relativistic corrections become important for an electron?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
For an electron, \(m = 9.11 \times 10^{-31}\text{ kg}\), \(c = 3 \times 10^{8}\text{ m/s}\), and \(h = 6.626 \times 10^{-34}\text{ J}\cdot\text{s}\). Candidate wavelengths are \(10\text{ nm}\), \(10^{-3}\text{ nm}\), \(10^{-4}\text{ nm}\), and \(10^{-6}\text{ nm}\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
Relativistic corrections become important when the classical speed \(v = \frac{h}{m\lambda}\) becomes comparable to or exceeds \(c\) (so \(\frac{1}{2}mv^2\) is comparable to or exceeds \(mc^2\)).

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
From the de Broglie relation \(\lambda = \frac{h}{mv}\), the non-relativistic speed estimate is \(v = \frac{h}{m\lambda}\).

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Computing \(v\) for each wavelength:
- For \(\lambda = 10\text{ nm} = 10^{-8}\text{ m}\): \(v = \frac{6.626 \times 10^{-34}}{9.11 \times 10^{-31} \times 10^{-8}} \approx 7.3 \times 10^{4}\text{ m/s} \ll c\) (non-relativistic).
- For \(\lambda = 10^{-3}\text{ nm} = 10^{-12}\text{ m}\): \(v \approx 7.3 \times 10^{8}\text{ m/s}\), which is on the order of \(c\) (boundary regime, whereas the Compton wavelength is \(\lambda_C = \frac{h}{mc} \approx 2.4 \times 10^{-3}\text{ nm}\)).
- For \(\lambda = 10^{-4}\text{ nm} = 10^{-13}\text{ m}\): \(v \approx 7.3 \times 10^{9}\text{ m/s} \gg c\).
- For \(\lambda = 10^{-6}\text{ nm} = 10^{-15}\text{ m}\): \(v \approx 7.3 \times 10^{11}\text{ m/s} \gg c\).

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Since no particle can exceed \(c\), classical formulas break down completely at \(\lambda = 10^{-4}\text{ nm}\) and \(\lambda = 10^{-6}\text{ nm}\) (well below the Compton wavelength). Therefore, relativistic corrections are definitely important at \(\lambda = 10^{-4}\text{ nm}\) and \(\lambda = 10^{-6}\text{ nm}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_MCQII_DUALNATUREOFRADIATIONANDMATTER_MCQ_Q11_10 - Particles of different masses with same de Broglie wavelength

questiontext.text: 11.10 Two particles \(A_1\), and \(A_2\) of masses \(m_1, m_2\) (\(m_1 > m_2\)) have the same de Broglie wavelength. Then

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Two particles \(A_1\) and \(A_2\) have masses \(m_1\) and \(m_2\) with \(m_1 > m_2\), and equal de Broglie wavelengths \(\lambda_1 = \lambda_2 = \lambda\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
Both particles are non-relativistic, so kinetic energy is \(E = \frac{p^2}{2m}\).

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
The de Broglie relation gives momentum \(p = \frac{h}{\lambda}\), and kinetic energy in terms of momentum is \(E = \frac{p^2}{2m}\).

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Since \(\lambda_1 = \lambda_2\), their momenta are \(p_1 = \frac{h}{\lambda_1} = \frac{h}{\lambda_2} = p_2\), so their momenta are the same. For the same momentum \(p\), the kinetic energy is \(E = \frac{p^2}{2m} \propto \frac{1}{m}\). Because \(m_1 > m_2\), it follows that \(E_1 < E_2\), meaning the energy of \(A_1\) is less than the energy of \(A_2\).

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Both conclusions follow directly from \(p = h/\lambda\) and \(E = p^2/(2m)\). Therefore, their momenta are the same, and the energy of \(A_1\) is less than the energy of \(A_2\).

answer.text: energy of \(A_1\) is less than the energy of \(A_2\).
energy of \(A_1\) is more than the energy of \(A_2\).

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_MCQII_DUALNATUREOFRADIATIONANDMATTER_MCQ_Q11_11 - Photon and electron de Broglie wavelength comparison

questiontext.text: 11.11 The de Broglie wavelength of a photon is twice the de Broglie wavelength of an electron. The speed of the electron is \(v_e = \frac{c}{100}\). Then

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
The photon wavelength \(\lambda_p\) and electron de Broglie wavelength \(\lambda_e\) satisfy \(\lambda_p = 2\lambda_e\). The electron speed is \(v_e = \frac{c}{100}\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
Since \(v_e = 0.01c \ll c\), the electron is non-relativistic, so \(p_e = m_e v_e\) and its kinetic energy is \(E_e = \frac{1}{2}m_e v_e^2\).

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
The de Broglie relation gives \(p = \frac{h}{\lambda}\). For a photon, \(E_p = p_p c = \frac{hc}{\lambda_p}\). For the electron, \(E_e = \frac{1}{2}m_e v_e^2 = \frac{1}{2}p_e v_e\).

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
First, the electron momentum ratio is \(\frac{p_e}{m_e c} = \frac{m_e v_e}{m_e c} = \frac{v_e}{c} = \frac{1}{100} = 10^{-2}\). Second, since \(\lambda_p = 2\lambda_e\), the photon momentum is \(p_p = \frac{h}{\lambda_p} = \frac{h}{2\lambda_e} = \frac{p_e}{2}\). Therefore, the photon energy is \(E_p = p_p c = \frac{1}{2}p_e c\). Taking the energy ratio gives \(\frac{E_e}{E_p} = \frac{\frac{1}{2}p_e v_e}{\frac{1}{2}p_e c} = \frac{v_e}{c} = \frac{1}{100} = 10^{-2}\).

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Both ratios are dimensionless and equal to \(\frac{v_e}{c} = 10^{-2}\). Hence, \(\frac{E_e}{E_p} = 10^{-2}\) and \(\frac{p_e}{m_e c} = 10^{-2}\).

questiontext.text: 11.12 Photons absorbed in matter are converted to heat. A source emitting \(n\) photon/sec of frequency \(\nu\) is used to convert \(1\text{ kg}\) of ice at \(0^\circ\text{C}\) to water at \(0^\circ\text{C}\). Then, the time \(T\) taken for the conversion

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Mass of ice \(m = 1 ext{ kg}\) at \(0^\circ ext{C}\) is converted to water at \(0^\circ ext{C}\) by a source emitting \(n\) photons per second, each of frequency \( u\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
All emitted photons are absorbed and converted completely into latent heat of fusion \(L\) of ice.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
Heat required to melt mass \(m\) of ice is \(Q = mL\). Energy of one photon is \(E = h u\), so the total energy delivered in time \(T\) is \(E_{ ext{total}} = n T h u\).

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Equating heat required to energy supplied gives \(mL = n T h u\), so \(T = rac{mL}{n h u}\). Since \(m\), \(L\), and \(h\) are constants, \(T \propto rac{1}{n u}\). Thus:
- With \( u\) fixed, \(T \propto rac{1}{n}\), so \(T\) decreases as \(n\) increases.
- With \(n\) fixed, \(T \propto rac{1}{ u}\), so \(T\) decreases as \( u\) increases.
- If \(n\) and \( u\) change such that \(n u = ext{constant}\), then \(T\) remains constant.
- If the product \(n u\) increases, \(T\) decreases rather than increases.

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Higher power \(P = nh u\) melts the ice faster. Therefore, \(T\) decreases with increasing \(n\) (at fixed \( u\)), decreases with increasing \( u\) (at fixed \(n\)), and remains constant when \(n u = ext{constant}\).

answer.text: remains constant with \(n\) and \(\nu\) changing such that \(n\nu = \text{constant}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_MCQII_DUALNATUREOFRADIATIONANDMATTER_MCQ_Q11_13 - De Broglie wavelength in central force orbit

questiontext.text: 11.13 A particle moves in a closed orbit around the origin, due to a force which is directed towards the origin. The de Broglie wavelength of the particle varies cyclically between two values \(\lambda_1\), \(\lambda_2\) with \(\lambda_1 > \lambda_2\). Which of the following statement are true?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
A particle moving in a closed orbit under a central force directed towards the origin conserves angular momentum \(\mathbf{L} = \mathbf{r} \times \mathbf{p}\), and its de Broglie wavelength \(\lambda = \frac{h}{mv}\) is inversely proportional to its speed \(v\).

Step 2: Evaluation
In a circular orbit with the origin at the centre, the distance \(r\) and speed \(v\) are constant everywhere, so \(\lambda\) would remain constant rather than varying cyclically between \(\lambda_1\) and \(\lambda_2\). Thus, the orbit cannot be circular with the origin as centre, and instead can be an elliptical orbit with the origin as a focus.

Step 3: Application
At the nearest point (perihelion) and farthest point (aphelion) of an elliptical orbit, the velocity is perpendicular to the radius vector, so angular momentum magnitude is \(L = mvr = \text{constant}\). Hence \(v \propto \frac{1}{r}\), which implies \(\lambda = \frac{h}{mv} \propto r\). Since \(\lambda_1 > \lambda_2\), the smaller wavelength \(\lambda_2\) corresponds to the higher speed and therefore the smaller distance \(r\) from the origin.

Step 4: Final Conclusion
Therefore, the particle could be moving in an elliptic orbit with the origin as its focus, and when the de Broglie wavelength is \(\lambda_2\), the particle is nearer the origin than when its value is \(\lambda_1\).

answer.text: The particle could be moving in a circular orbit with origin as centre
The particle could be moving in an elliptic orbit with origin as its focus.
When the de Broglie wave length is \(\lambda_1\), the particle is nearer the origin than when its value is \(\lambda_2\).
When the de Broglie wavelength is \(\lambda_2\), the particle is nearer the origin than when its value is \(\lambda_1\).
